sources.authors: Bratthall, Figueira, Nording
sources.source_byte_caveat: PMC peer-reviewed original full HTML directly inspected 2026-11-09, PubMed PMID 38434259 and Umea/SciLifeLab indexed identity crosschecked; HTML/PDF binary not downloaded or SHA-256 hashed. Original figures and supplementary raw tables not reanalyzed.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Bratthall, Figueira, Nording, Heliyon 10(5) e26625 (online Feb 17 2024; collection Mar 15). Methods: one dark 100% Arabica commercial blend coarse French-press grind, 11g/200mL, 93C, five minute immersion/filter, 9 groups (pure-water control; MgCl2/CaCl2 100/1000ppm as salts either before or after brew) n=5/group. Four measured organic acids citric/malic/lactic/quinic using GC-MS and NMR; 100ppm salts produced little/no change in measured acids, most pre/post comparisons similar; at 1000ppm analytical methods diverged, with salt-induced complexation/spectral effects possible. Bicarbonate/normal mixed water ions excluded. No espresso brewing, five-taste sensory experiment, subjective acidity perception or measured espresso recipe outcome. Cannot treat ppm of chloride SALT as ppm of elemental magnesium/calcium, assert water-independent flavor or universal mineral dose.

Original Cell/Matter search-indexed article text substantively read 2026-11-10 with Introduction, Development of Rational Model, Effect of Brew Ratio and Pressure, Brewing Espresso, Systematically Improving Espresso, Implementation and Outlook. Direct DOI open returned 403; original contiguous HTML, accepted-manuscript PDF byte hash, figure pixels, supplemental equations/raw replicate measurements and consumer ratings NOT independently verified. sources.claims_verified_externally: Original author's homogeneous-flow mathematical model predicts greater EY with finer grind, while the cafe experiment under 6 bar (lowered from 9 bar because of fine-grind clogging) observes a peaked EY-versus-grind relationship with lower EY/greater variation at very fine settings. Within tested setup, automated 98 N tamp had no appreciable observed shot time/EY variation; the authors explicitly did not quantify observed flavor changes. A 20g-to-15g dose reduction/coarser-grind cafe protocol, shorter ~14s shots and sales-based coffee-cost case illustrate operational efficiency, NOT randomized preferred espresso flavor or personal five-input DIC outcomes. EY/TDS, time, taste and economic success are different measured outcomes, and neither fine-grind 'critical point' nor a brew-time target transfers universally across grinders, burrs, coffees, feeds, pressure and baskets.

sources.claims_verified_externally: Author original manuscript Methods 2.4-2.7 and Results 3.1-3.7: single dark roasted Arabica, EK43/Vario grounds, 6 PSDs from coarse mean alpha approx 224/296/427 micrometers and width/uniformity beta 1.40/1.95 with fines below 100 micrometers held about 25+/-4%, three compression trials per distribution, powder rheometer 2-75 kPa and separate texture analyzer, modified Bezzera BZ09 at approximately 88+/-2 C with 50 g collected beverage. Both PSD width and mean size interact with dry compressed bed porosity and steady-state permeability: low permeability not exclusive to fine mean size. Extraction permeability calculated from pressure and flow averaged from about 10 seconds after onset, not a time-resolved cup sensory model. Fitted Kozeny-Carman terms are experiment-dependent; conclusion explicitly flags other water temperatures, coffee roast, fines fraction and portafilter geometry as future validation limits. No consumer taste outcome, DIC all-five sensory trial, universal compression or grind optimum.

sources.claims_verified_externally: Three different coffees (Ethiopia light natural, Kenya medium washed, Starbucks mainstream dark) were compared across eight non-espresso brew systems (AeroPress/Chemex/Clever/French Press/Moka/Pure Brew/Ibrik/V60), with three preparation replicates per method, HPLC-DAD acids/caffeine and twelve trained panelists rating perceived acidity/mouthfeel. Authors report pH and titratable acidity linked to CQAs while organic acids correlate more with perceived sourness in specialty samples; TA versus sensory acidity r reported light 0.6638, medium 0.3268, dark 0.8516 across the 8 method observations. Coffee identity, processing and roast differ together; no espresso shots, individual preferences or universal one-to-one pH-to-sourness conversion tested.
sources.source_byte_caveat: Original publisher indexed article sections read from web snippets; direct publisher webpage blocked 403, no complete original binary, supplements or raw subject ratings verified; PDF university repository listed open but not downloaded. Simonelli Group partially funded first author's PhD and aided coffee preparation; no known conflicts declared.

sources.title: Brew temperature, at fixed brew strength and extraction, has little impact on the sensory profile of drip brew coffee
sources.authors: Mackenzie E. Batali; William D. Ristenpart; Jean-Xavier Guinard
sources.methods_verified: Original full open-access PMC HTML: one washed coffee, commercial Curtis G4 flat-bottom paper filter brewer, 3 temperatures 87/90/93 C x 9 TDS/PE target coordinates = 27 sample types; 270 separate brews total. Fig2 caption separately reports n=9 for each target brew, which does not arithmetically explain 270 across 27 types; full replicate-count reconciliation to supplement remains OPEN. Brewer grind, dose, flow and brew time adjusted to match targets; 12 trained panelists 19-30 years; randomized blinded Williams Latin Square, red-lit booths, triplicate descriptive 31-attribute evaluation. All servings 65 +/-1 C. See https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7536440/ lines 120-122, 164-175, 288-318.
sources.findings_verified: Full original PMC results Table 2: brew temperature MANOVA F=1.25, p=0.11; TDS F=5.44, p<0.001 and PE F=2.46, p<0.001; one univariate attribute Nutty temperature difference only 1/100 score, possible type-I; 2020 authors explicitly caution the effect and brewing-method limits. This is drip and cannot negate espresso effects or imply universal preference.
sources.correction_verified: Original Methods/Coffee water recipe had a published typographical error: 1.16g CaSO4.2H2O, 4.97g MgSO4, 3.26g NaHCO3, 2.57g KHCO3 per L should read per 100 L (official 2021-01-25 Author Correction, PMC7835346). No experimental water recipe or mineral recommendation for DIC created.
sources.caveats: Original publisher URL redirected/blocked but full original open-access text is DIRECTLY accessible from PubMed Central PMC7536440 and read here; no original PDF bytes, supplementary raw table S1/S2 or primary study-wide raw data hash verified; per-target versus 270 brews counts unresolved from paper text; one coffee, drip not espresso. Published author correction per 100 L incorporated and independently read at PMC7835346.

sources.claims_verified_externally: Same washed Colombian Arabica and 20.00 +/-0.01 g dose, one DE1 Pro/IMS basket and Mahlkoenig E65S grinding at displayed levels 1.4/1.7/2.0; 15 face-centered DoE factor sets, triplicates except six center replicates; measured flow approximately 0.96/1.9/2.8 mL/s and measured water approximately 79.1/88.2/96.5 C. Ten fractions collected, six HPLC/TDS fractions assessed; measured trigonelline, caffeine, 5-CQA and TDS, not human taste. Across the studied domain flow effects interacted with grind and temperature; beverage mass (20/40/60g modeled cup outputs) had larger effects than individual operating settings. No universal five-taste recommendations or optimal espresso temperature established.

sources.claims_verified_externally: Study uses one Central American 2-bean blend, split to light and darker medium-dark roasts, 4/22/92C water, 5 time points each, coarse 972 +/-19um median grind, 100g grounds and 500g water in nonpressurized Toddy cupping immersion. sources.source_byte_caveat: Publisher complete HTML read and metadata crosschecked against OpenAlex bibliographic entry; version-of-record PDF binary not downloaded/hashed, original figure pixels and raw triangle/preference responses not independently reanalyzed; datasets available by request to lead author, no independent replication verified. sources.claims_verified_externally: Publisher Materials/Methods: same 2018/19 harvest Mexican single-estate pulped-natural Catuai with one batch roasted 1 day and another 145 days before tasting (two event dates in 2024); caffe-creme-style 50:50 light/dark roast blend brewed on Franke S700 15 g in/140 mL water, 40 s, 90 C, served approx 60 +/- 5 C, not the DIC standard espresso shot. At coffee events 60 untrained participants used triangle discrimination ISO 4120: 42/60 identified different sample (70%, p<.001 vs 1/3 guessing). Only those 42 then gave forced relative preference: 22/42 older vs 20/42 fresh, p=.875. Non-significant binomial preference is NOT equivalence, proof of unchanged flavor, absolute liking or an optimal rest window. No 2-14-day age series, DIC five input ratings, same-person recipe adjustments, blind espresso machine style comparison or roast-specific preferred aging windows; storage, roasting batch effects, volunteer recruitment and data-on-request limit inference. Coauthor reports ownership of Coffee Consulate; study declares no external funding.

sources.title: The clean taste of coffee depends on the sodium content of its extraction water
sources.authors: Koji Imamura
sources.direct_review_provenance: Original J-STAGE article lines 12-39 identity; 72-87 abstract/introduction; 88-121 methods; 122-170 water/sensory/sensor results; 171-204 measured compounds/sodium experiment; 213-239 Table 4/conclusion; 240 acknowledgments. Original publisher release 2024-03-19 and DOI, not copy from secondary reports.
sources.source_byte_caveat: One mocha Arabica blend; 28 g grounds/515 mL, coffee maker extraction at 78 C, NOT espresso. Six trained volunteers in blind ratings; JCQA check-count positive/negative items, not validated DIC five 1-5 scales. Sensors TS-5000Z averaged three stabilized readings, HPLC/cation/anion testing. Comparisons span source water and chlorine as well as sodium; sodium citrate manipulation cannot isolate every potential taste effect; small panel, no same-person espresso outcome or repeatability study. Author is affiliated with an ice manufacturer; acknowledging industry context is not proof of research misconduct. Journal HTML full body directly read; original PDF binary/figure pixels/raw replicates not independently inspected or byte-hashed. Main narrative calls four water types while listing five including ultrapure, so enumerate actual treatments carefully.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Ground Brazil/Ethiopia blend 28g/515mL at 78 C via drip machine. Melted-ice water (<0.1 ppm Na) gave six of six positive clean evaluations vs one for ground water and three for tap, and high combined JCQA score (Table 3), but check-counts are not independent continuous taste magnitudes. Across studied brewed coffees, sodium (0.49/7.02/2.06/0.86 ppm) differed with water, while caffeine and chlorogenic acid differences were reported nonsignificant. Sodium-citrate added at 0.75 ppm to melted-ice water reduced six-person clean positive count 4 to 2 in a later table (Table 4); TS-5000Z sensor saltiness response significant, other seven sensor outputs not significant in this manipulation. Do not infer optimal espresso minerals, machine-safe water, DIC clarity scale, universal sodium thresholds, or chemical-to-subjective-score causality.

sources.title: Effect of Temperature and Storage on Coffee’s Volatile Compound Profile and Sensory Characteristics
sources.authors: Magdalena Gantner; Eliza Kostyra; Elżbieta Górska-Horczyczak; Anna Piotrowska
sources.direct_review_provenance: Publisher HTML (2026-11-10 retrieval): lines 143-180 identity/abstract, 197-229 original Methods, 230-276 Results/figures and table captions, 290-334 Discussion/Conclusions, 335-355 Funding/COI. Tables 1-4 actual cells and figure pixels were NOT independently read. Cross-checked current live source and active Locked supersessions, not a new owner policy. No local publisher HTML/PDF byte download or cryptographic SHA256.
sources.source_byte_caveat: Source publisher HTML read via web extraction, not byte frozen; original 21-page PDF, actual Table 1-4 numeric cells, Figure 1-3 pixels, original GC peak integrations, participants' individual sensory records and independent replication NOT inspected. Do not infer universal post-roast resting time, shelf life, ideal 5 C household storage, zero fridge-moisture risk, or a DIC recommendation effect.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Commercial 100% Arabica, 100% Robusta and 80:20 blend; roaster did not provide specific origins/roasting profiles. Bags were first opened one month after roasting; then compared fresh-opened with one additional month sealed in foil at 5±1 C or 20±1 C. Espresso made in a DeLonghi automatic with stated 20 g for 2x40 mL and manufacturer dial 1, not a controlled 1:2 personal espresso workflow; cold brew was different 300 g/1200 mL, 24h at 5 C. Espresso served 60±2 C, cold brew 5±2 C. QDA used 30 trained-panel descriptors on anchored 0-10 cm scales, duplicate sample analysis with an average 18 evaluations; neither 18 individuals nor DIC's five independent preferences should be inferred. Authors report espresso differences in coffee aroma/flavor, chocolate odor, sour/sweet taste and body across sample combinations (Table 3 named p-values), but also state post-open espresso brews at BOTH storage temperatures differed from fresh and were similar to one another; reduced storage-temperature alteration is clearer in volatile signals and cold brew. Text §3.2 unexpectedly says stored at 7 C, inconsistent with Methods' 5±1 C; the methods are the stated condition, not grounds for inventing a third group. This study does not compare different resting dates immediately after roast or assess the same person's DIC shot recommendations.
